title: Breakup of the big band and joining Sidney Bechet
summary: With big bands failing in 1947 Moore was jobless; Sidney Bechet hired him and taught him traditional jazz.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I see. Okay. That band was together until -- you were in it up to the summer of 1947, then what happened?

1947. /We were beginning to see signs of whatever you call it, the handwriting on the wall. All the bands were breaking up. It was an economic situation where big bands were getting out of style. Everybody was making small bands. So that left me

without a job and everybody cut out and that broke up the band, Joe Glaser -- and that's the time that Louie had this band and he had, and I don't remember who was the first ones, it was a small band. I think Teagarden.
Teagarden probably was one of them.

There was only about five of them now left us, the only way they'd do it, now we scrounged ourselves around New York, that's how I got to traditional jazz because it was Sidney Bechet who hired me without even thinking, he didn't know that I don't know how to play traditional jazz and he came to me and said, "How would you like to work with me?" So I told him that I didn't know traditional jazz like he did. "That's all right, I like your tone. give you your notes." Which he did. He's so great, Bechet is. Experienced. And he'd be playing "Muskrat Ramble" he'd be giving me my notes while he's taking off. That's how great he was. Well in between working with Bechet I was in the Central Plaza, Second Avenue and the Stuyvesant Casino and then there came the Metropole. I was a guest artist along with Bud Freeman and Punch Miller, Al Assen at one time was the guest of Eddie Condon, I'm speaking about Eddie Condon, the old Eddie Condon which was then in the Village in those days. Johnny Winters was a guest there, Johnny Mintz different guys.
